470.title: Ashtpadi 9, salok: the true names
470.hook: the salok turns to what the true devotee is like
470.howItsDone: Sikhism has no priestly caste: any Sikh may read the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs read ashtpadi nine of Sukhmani Sahib as a call to live up to a name rather than rest on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gareebee: a child in her father's shoes, and a portrait to grow into. Your line was grow into it. Today, ashtpadi nine.

Every age has its religious job titles. Reverend. Doctor of divinity. Elder. In Guru Arjan's Punjab, around 1600, people heard plenty too: pandit, the learned one; vaishnav, the devotee of Vishnu; and aparas, the untouched one, a holy man who kept himself ritually apart, never touching anything that might make him impure. Ashtpadi nine takes these honored names one by one. It doesn't mock them. It does something more interesting: it asks what each name would look like if it were true all the way through.
screen: `EVERY AGE HAS ITS TITLES.` → `PANDIT, VAISHNAV, APARAS.` → `WHAT IF EACH WERE TRUE?`

segments.voice: The salok begins with the last of those names. Whoever keeps the Name enshrined in the heart, sees God in everyone, and bows to the Master moment by moment: Nanak, that one is the true aparas, and saves all. Notice the swap. The aparas of the day kept apart from other people to stay pure. Guru Arjan's aparas sees God in everyone, the opposite of keeping apart. The purity is still there, but it's moved: not what your hands avoid, but what your heart holds. The first stanza fills it in: the true aparas is one whose tongue never touches a lie, whose eyes don't look with lust at another's spouse, who loves the company of the holy. The untouched one is untouched by falsehood. That's the pattern of the whole ashtpadi. Each stanza takes a respected title and pours new content into it, a life to match the name. It says nothing against the people who held those titles sincerely. It just won't let the name do the work by itself. This fits the Sikh path closely. Sikhism has no priestly caste. A granthi who reads in the gurdwara is a respected servant of the community, not a holy class apart, and any Sikh, woman or man, may read the Guru Granth Sahib. So ashtpadi nine keeps asking not what are you called, but what are you like.

segments.voice: Picture someone with an impressive title, a doctor, a judge, a religious leader, and then someone with no title at all who is completely trustworthy, and ask which one you'd call at two in the morning. Let that answer settle, then turn the question, gently, toward yourself: not what you're called, but what you're like when no one's watching.
Aparas, the untouched one. Not the one who keeps apart, but the one who sees God in all.
Your line: true, not titled. A name is only as true as the life under it. See you tomorrow.

471.title: The true scholar
471.hook: the true pandit is one who instructs his own mind
471.howItsDone: Sikhs value study of Gurbani through katha and personal reading, and read this stanza of Sukhmani Sahib as a reminder that learning should first change the learner.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aparas: the true untouched one, untouched by falsehood, seeing God in all. Your line was true, not titled. Today, ashtpadi nine takes up another title: the scholar.

A friend can win any argument and still can't stop checking his phone at dinner. A brilliant expert gives wonderful advice and never takes any of it. A teacher explains patience beautifully and loses her temper at the photocopier. Knowing a lot and being changed by what you know are two very different things. In the Guru's day, the pandit was the learned one, the scholar who knew the old texts and taught them. Ashtpadi nine asks: who does the true pandit teach first?
screen: `WINS EVERY ARGUMENT.` → `NEVER TAKES HIS OWN ADVICE.` → `WHO DOES THE PANDIT TEACH FIRST?`

segments.voice: The stanza opens: so pandit jo man parbodhai. That one is a pandit who instructs his own mind. Parbodh means to awaken, to teach, to bring to understanding. The first student is the self. Next: he searches for the Lord's Name within his own soul. Then: he drinks the sweet essence of the Name, and by that pandit's teaching the world lives. And a line that shows this pandit isn't rejecting learning: he understands the root of the old scriptures, and sees the large hidden in the small. So the true scholar still reads, but the reading has gone inward first and come back out as a life. Then a line with real weight in a society ordered by caste: he gives teaching to all four castes. Chahu varnaa: all four. The stanza's ideal scholar teaches everyone. Sikh practice carries that on: the Guru Granth Sahib, written in Gurmukhi script in the spoken languages of its time, is read aloud to anyone who walks into the gurdwara. The stanza ends with Nanak bowing, forever, to that kind of pandit. So the order matters: teach your own mind first, and then your teaching might keep the world alive. This isn't anti-intellectual. Sikh tradition honors its scholars, poets and scribes. It's about which direction the learning flows.

segments.voice: Pick a piece of advice you often give other people, slow down, drink water, don't take it personally, and say it now, silently, to yourself, as both the teacher and the student. Then ask your mind, kindly, did you hear that, and sit with the answer without scolding. If you pray, you can ask for an awakened mind.
Pandit, a learned person. So pandit jo man parbodhai: the real pandit is the one who instructs his own mind, and then teaches everyone.
Your line: teach your own mind. The first student is always the self. That's day four hundred seventy-one.

472.title: The true devotee
472.hook: titles mean nothing without the life that matches
472.howItsDone: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara and beyond, and read these stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib as describing devotion that seeks no reward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pandit: the scholar who teaches his own mind first. Your line was teach your own mind. Today, ashtpadi nine turns to the devotee.

Someone volunteers at a shelter every Saturday, and makes sure to post a photo every time. Someone else drives an elderly neighbor to the doctor every month for years and never mentions it to anyone. Both did good. Photos aren't wicked. But only one of the two is plainly not waiting for anything back. Ashtpadi nine has two stanzas about devotees, and both land on exactly that point.
screen: `A PHOTO EVERY SATURDAY.` → `A NEIGHBOR DRIVEN FOR YEARS.` → `WHO WASN'T WAITING FOR ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: One stanza takes the title vaishnav, a devotee of Vishnu, an honored name. The true vaishnav, it says, is the one with whom God is well pleased, who lives apart from the pull of maya, the passing world. Then the striking line: karam karat hovai nihkaram. Doing deeds, he remains without deeds. Nihkaram means free of the deed, free of its grip. It doesn't mean doing nothing. It means doing the good thing without hooking yourself to the result. The next lines say it plainly: he doesn't hanker after the fruit of any action; he is absorbed only in devotion and the singing of praise. The next stanza takes another devotee's title, bhagauti, and says the same in a different key: the true one is dyed in love for God, leaves bad company behind, and every doubt dissolves from the mind. Two titles, one point. Devotion is measured by the life underneath it, and especially by whether it's waiting for a reward. The neighbor who drives someone to the doctor for years isn't keeping score. The deed is done; the doer isn't clinging. This isn't a criticism of the people who held these titles; the stanzas honor the names by asking them to be true. It's a mirror, held up to anyone who calls themselves devoted, in any community. Sikhs have a word for selfless service, seva, and its whole point is the same: the life, not the title.

segments.voice: Choose one value you care about, kindness, honesty, patience, and picture one small act of it that no one will see, like wiping a shared table or leaving a good review for a stranger's small shop. Notice any little wish to be noticed, and let it go on the out-breath. Breathe in: the deed; breathe out: no reward.
Nihkaram, free of the deed. Doing deeds, yet free of them, hankering after no reward.
Your line: the life, not the title. The deed is done, and the doer isn't clinging. Until tomorrow.

473.title: Living ashtpadi 9
473.hook: drop one title and keep the substance
473.howItsDone: Sikhs use the names Singh and Kaur, which tradition links to the founding of the Khalsa, in place of or alongside family surnames, and read ashtpadi nine of Sukhmani Sahib as a call to substance over status.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nihkaram: doing deeds, free of them, seeking no reward. Your line was the life, not the title. Today, ashtpadi nine, lived.

A Sikh family is introduced at a wedding. Harpreet Kaur, her husband Jaswant Singh, their son Arjun Singh, their daughter Simran Kaur, and the grandmother, also a Kaur. Then the woman from another village who runs the langar kitchen: Kaur again. Elsewhere, a surname can tell a stranger your caste, your clan, your rank. These two names are shared on purpose, and they tell the room nothing of the kind. That's ashtpadi nine, carried into everyday life.
screen: `A FAMILY OF SINGHS AND KAURS.` → `SURNAMES THAT TELL YOUR RANK.` → `NAMES THAT DELIBERATELY DON'T.`

segments.voice: Ashtpadi nine took the honored titles of its day, the aparas, the vaishnav, the bhagauti, the pandit, and poured a matching life into each one. Untouched by falsehood. Doing good, not gripped by reward. Teaching your own mind first. Stanza after stanza: the name is nothing without the substance underneath it. Later, Sikh tradition remembers Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, making that idea visible. Tradition says that when he founded the Khalsa, he gave the initiated men the name Singh, meaning lion, and the women the name Kaur, often explained as princess. The same names for everyone, whatever family or caste they came from. Today some Sikhs use Singh or Kaur in place of a caste surname, and others carry them alongside a family name; there's real variety. But the idea behind the custom is the one Guru Arjan was teaching in Sukhmani: titles that rank people don't decide who someone is. For any of us, living ashtpadi nine can be smaller than a new name. It can be letting go of one title in your own head: the clever one, the responsible one, the one who's always right, the expert. Not the work behind it, just the label. Keep the substance. Drop the badge.

segments.voice: Name to yourself one title you quietly carry, the smart one, the fixer, the good one, the busy one, and imagine setting it down beside you like a heavy bag. Breathe, and ask who you are without it; probably the same person, just lighter. If you pray, you can offer your good deeds without your name on them.
Singh, lion. The name given at the Khalsa's founding, the same for everyone, whatever caste: drop one title, keep the substance.
Your line: substance over title. People know you best by how you live. Day four hundred seventy-three, done.

474.title: Ashtpadi 10, salok: countless
474.hook: the salok marvels at countless beings
474.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani Sahib meet this salok at the opening of the tenth ashtpadi, whose stanzas go on to list the countless beings of the creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Singh and Kaur, and a badge set down. Your line was substance over title. Today, ashtpadi ten, and the camera pulls back.

Rush hour at a train station. A flood of people, every one the main character of their own story. One is late for a job interview. One just got engaged. One is going to visit a mother in the hospital. One is humming. You'll never know any of them, and each carries an inner life as large as yours. A crowd like that can make a person feel very small, or strangely tender. For several ashtpadis, Sukhmani has zoomed in on one kind of person. Now it pulls back, and looks at the crowd.
screen: `A STATION AT RUSH HOUR.` → `EACH ONE A WHOLE STORY.` → `SUKHMANI PULLS BACK.`

segments.voice: The salok of ashtpadi ten has two lines. The first: ustat karahi anek jan. Countless people sing His praise. Ustat is praise; anek is many, more than one can number. And there's no end to it: ant na paaraavaar, no near bank or far bank. The second line: Nanak, God made the creation in so many ways, of countless kinds. Rachnaa is creation, the thing made, the way a poem or a building is made. Bahu bidh, many ways. Anik prakaar, countless kinds. Notice what's being praised. Not one perfect person, not the brahm giaanee of two ashtpadis ago, but the sheer number and variety of what exists. In the stanzas that follow, Guru Arjan will list them: people who worship and people who wander, scholars and the lost, worlds beyond worlds. The salok sets the tone for all of it, and the tone is wonder. So many. When you really take that in, something shifts. Your own problems are still real, but they're one story among millions. The people who annoy you are also among the so many, each with a whole inner life. And the One who made the creation in all those ways is, the salok says, beyond any shore you could reach. Here the crowd isn't a reason to feel lost. It's a reason for wonder, and everyone in it is part of the same creation.
screen: `USTAT: COUNTLESS PEOPLE PRAISE.` · `NO END, NO FAR SHORE.` · `RACHNAA: A CREATION OF MANY KINDS.` · `ONE STORY AMONG MILLIONS.` · then, large: `SO MANY.`

segments.voice: Look out a window at people passing, or at faces in a photo, or, eyes closed, picture a busy street you know, and pick out one stranger. Imagine, just for a breath, that they too woke up this morning with worries and hopes, then another, then another, and let your face soften as you look. If you pray, you can wish them well in your own words.
Rachnaa, the creation, the thing made. Its salok marvels at countless people praising, and a rachnaa made in so many ways.
Your line: so many. Every one of them a whole story, and all of it one creation. See you tomorrow.

475.title: Many millions
475.hook: kaee kott: many millions worship, many millions wander, many millions are learned
475.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani Sahib recite the 'kaee kot' stanzas of the tenth ashtpadi in a strong, repeated rhythm, as a hymn of wonder at the size of the creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rachnaa: countless people praising, a creation of countless kinds. Your line was so many. Today the stanzas start counting.

In India, big numbers have their own names. A lakh is a hundred thousand. A crore is ten million. Headlines say a film earned a hundred crore; a festival drew two crore pilgrims. In Punjabi and in the old language of the Guru Granth Sahib, the word is kot, or kott. And ashtpadi ten picks up that enormous number and swings it like a drumstick. Kaee kot. Many crores. Many tens of millions. Line after line, in a rhythm you can feel even if you don't understand a single word.
screen: `A LAKH, A CRORE.` → `KOT: TEN MILLION.` → `KAEE KOT, LINE AFTER LINE.`

segments.voice: The first stanza runs like this. Kaee kot hoe poojaaree: many millions are worshippers. Many millions keep religious rites and customs. Many millions live at places of pilgrimage. Many millions wander the forests as renunciates. Many millions listen to the Vedas. Many millions become great ascetics. Many millions fix their minds in meditation. Many millions are poets, pondering poetry. Many millions meditate on the ever-new Name. And the last line: Nanak, none of them can find the Creator's limit. Look who's in the list: every kind of seeker of Guru Arjan's world, and not one is mocked or ranked. They're simply counted, with wonder, as part of the creation. Then the turn. All those millions, every path of seeking, and none reaches the end of the One who made them. That's not a put-down of the seekers. It's a statement about how big the Creator is. If tens of millions of sincere seekers can't measure it, nobody is going to measure it alone. Japji, which we read last year, says it too: no one can reach the end of God's praise. Kaee kot is that same humility, set to a drumbeat. Millions upon millions, every one of them held. Millions, all His.
screen: `KAEE KOT: MANY TENS OF MILLIONS.` · `WORSHIPPERS, PILGRIMS, POETS.` · `COUNTED, NOT RANKED.` · `NONE FINDS THE CREATOR'S LIMIT.` · then, large: `MILLIONS, ALL HIS.`

segments.voice: Picture one person who prays differently from you, or doesn't pray at all, and wish them well: may they be safe, may they be at peace. Then widen the wish to a town, a country, the whole planet, eight billion, more than eight hundred crore; you can't picture every face, and that's the point. If you pray, you can hold them all before God.
Many millions. Kaee kot: tens of millions of seekers of every kind, counted with wonder, and none finding the Creator's limit.
Your line: millions, all his. Every path, every seeker, held. That's day four hundred seventy-five.

476.title: All in His creation
476.hook: the good and the lost are all within His play
476.howItsDone: Sikhs read this stanza of Sukhmani Sahib as a reminder that only the Creator knows the creation, while still standing against injustice as the Gurus taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many millions: worshippers, pilgrims, poets, counted with wonder. Your line was millions, all His. Today the count keeps going, into harder territory.

Yesterday's list was easy to love. Pilgrims. Poets. Meditators. If the stanza had stopped there, it would be a nice hymn about good people. It doesn't stop there. The second stanza keeps the same drumbeat, kaee kot, many millions, and turns it on everyone we'd rather leave out of the picture. The proud. The cruel. The thieves. The gossips. The ones chasing money until they drop. It's the kind of list you'd expect before a sermon about who's going to be punished. And that sermon never comes.
screen: `YESTERDAY'S LIST WAS EASY.` → `NOW THE PROUD, THE CRUEL.` → `THE SERMON NEVER COMES.`

segments.voice: The second stanza goes: many millions are proud. Many millions are blind and ignorant. Many millions are misers, hard of heart. Many millions are cold inside, without feeling. Many millions steal what belongs to others. Many millions slander others. Many millions toil for wealth. Many millions wander in foreign lands. Then the turn, addressed straight to God: whatever You attach them to, to that they are attached. And the last line: Nanak, only the Creator knows His own creation. No verdict. Nobody's sentenced. These too are in the creation, and the One who made it is the only one who truly knows it. That doesn't mean Sikh teaching shrugs at cruelty or theft. The Gurus spoke hard words against oppression and greed, and Sikhs are asked to stand up for those who are wronged. But this stanza is about something else: the urge to stand outside the creation and sort it into the saved and the lost, as if we had made it. Kartaa is the word for the Creator, the Doer. Only the Kartaa knows the creation; all of it is within His play. That's humbling, and oddly freeing: you don't have to be everybody's judge. And this is where the week ends. Seven days ago, the true aparas. Then pandit, nihkaram, Singh and Kaur and the badge set down. Then the crowd: so many, many millions, and today, all of them, in the play.
screen: `THE PROUD, THE CRUEL, THE THIEVES.` · `WHATEVER YOU ATTACH THEM TO.` · `ONLY THE CREATOR KNOWS IT.` · `NOT EVERYBODY'S JUDGE.` · then, large: `ALL IN THE PLAY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've been judging lately, a relative, a coworker, a stranger online, and without arguing with your judgment or pretending they're right, picture them inside the same creation as you, held by the same hands. Breathe in: they're in the play; breathe out: so am I. You can still disagree and still say no; you're only setting down the gavel for a while.
Kartaa, the Creator, the Doer. The proud and the lost, the cruel and the kind, many millions, all within His play; only the Kartaa knows it.
Your line: all in the play. Only the Kartaa knows the whole of it. Another week, done.

screen: `DAY 476 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK OF TRUE NAMES AND MANY MILLIONS.` → `TOMORROW: LIVING ASHTPADI 10.`

chat.says: Why does that stanza list thieves and cruel people without saying what should happen to them?
options: It ends: only the Creator knows His creation. Sorting everyone into saved and lost isn't ours.
Because the stanza says cruelty and theft don't really matter, so no one should speak up.
Because the stanza leaves the sentencing to us, and expects us to judge them ourselves.
chat.meaning: Nanak, only the Creator knows His own creation. No verdict: don't play the Creator, while still standing up for the wronged.
